label: Short-Wave Asymptotics
notes: Open by framing the appendix as the bridge between wave mechanics and ray mechanics. As the wavelength shrinks, a wave equation behaves more and more like a Hamiltonian system, and the whole apparatus of phase, rays, fronts, and Lagrangian manifolds emerges from a single small parameter. Promise the caustic as the climax.

label: The WKB Ansatz
notes: Explain that we substitute a single oscillating mode with slowly varying amplitude into the wave operator. The large frequency multiplies derivatives of the phase, so collecting powers of the small parameter forces the leading equation to constrain the phase and the next order to constrain the amplitude. Stress this is asymptotic, not convergent.

label: Eikonal Equation
notes: Highlight that the highest power of frequency must vanish identically, which produces the eikonal equation. Identify it with the time-independent Hamilton-Jacobi equation where the gradient of the phase plays the role of momentum. Emphasise that solving for the phase is exactly the classical mechanics problem hiding inside the wave equation.

label: Transport Equation
notes: Move to the next order in the small parameter, which gives a first-order linear equation for the amplitude. Interpret it as conservation of a probability or energy flux along the rays. The amplitude grows where rays converge and shrinks where they spread, which already foreshadows the blow-up at caustics.

label: Rays and Bicharacteristics
notes: Introduce rays as the characteristic curves of the eikonal equation, equivalently the projections of the bicharacteristic flow of the Hamiltonian onto configuration space. Write the canonical equations and stress that position and momentum evolve together in phase space, while the ray is only the shadow of that lifted trajectory.

label: Wave Fronts and Huygens
notes: Define wave fronts as level sets of the phase and show that rays cross them orthogonally in the standard isotropic case. Present Huygens' principle as the statement that each front is the envelope of small wavelets emitted from the previous front, and that this envelope construction is dual to advancing along the rays.

label: Lagrangian Manifold
notes: Lift the picture into phase space: the graph of the phase gradient is a Lagrangian manifold, a half-dimensional surface on which the symplectic form vanishes. Explain that the bicharacteristic flow preserves this manifold, so the right object to track is not the multivalued phase downstairs but the single smooth surface upstairs.

label: Caustics and Folds
notes: Now deliver the climax: where neighbouring rays cross, the projection of the Lagrangian manifold to configuration space becomes singular. These fold and cusp points form the caustic, the bright envelope of the ray family. Stress that the manifold itself stays smooth; only its shadow degenerates, which is why a global lift is needed.

label: Breakdown of WKB
notes: Explain why the simple ansatz fails at a caustic: the amplitude carries an inverse Jacobian of the ray map, and that Jacobian vanishes where rays focus. The naive solution blows up. The cure is to work in the momentum representation near the fold, where the same manifold projects without singularity.

label: Maslov Index
notes: Introduce the Maslov index as the integer counting how many times a ray touches the caustic, weighted by the type of fold. Each passage advances the phase by a quarter period, so the global asymptotic solution is a sum over branches of the Lagrangian manifold with these phase jumps inserted. This fixes the quantization conditions.

label: Notebook Diagnostic
notes: Connect to the companion notebook, which renders the central object and records a finite diagnostic as a miniature contract. Invite learners to perturb the ray family, watch the caustic envelope move, and confirm the recorded invariant stays finite. Frame the check as a small proof obligation rather than decoration.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by retracing the ladder: ansatz, eikonal, transport, rays, fronts, Lagrangian lift, caustic, Maslov correction. Emphasise that semiclassical analysis turns a hard wave problem into geometry on phase space, and that the same scaffold underlies optics, quantum mechanics, and the stationary phase method used throughout the book.
